title: Drug contamination remediation
audience: Coordinators, supervisors and trained workers who may be asked to assess, triage, refer or document drug-related contamination in residential, rental or commercial premises. Not a qualification or authority to investigate, sample, decontaminate or certify any property.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: WA Health, Testing and remediation of methylamphetamine and illicit drug residues (last reviewed 21 May 2026; no published or updated date shown); WA Health, Clandestine drug laboratories and cleaning contamination (last reviewed 22 May 2026; no published or updated date shown); NZ Tenancy Services, Guidelines on meth contamination (last updated 9 October 2026).

subLessons.title: Independent sampling and chain of custody
Worker exposure prevention and PPE decisions

learningOutcomes: Define the scope of a drug-contamination request, separating what is known from what is reported, and identify the limits that stop the work.
Identify the authority that controls access and the written release required before any assessment or physical work.
Explain the routes by which contamination can spread and why uncertainty is never treated as safety.
Distinguish, at the level of recognition, a suspected clandestine laboratory from residue associated with use, and escalate the first to emergency services and specialists.
Explain why sampling, laboratory testing and chain of custody belong to independent, qualified professionals.
Explain why PPE and entry controls depend on a formal assessment and trained operators, and why improvised PPE is refused.
Set containment and cross-contamination boundaries, and recognise when a supervised zone or handoff is needed.
Recognise material decisions that need a specialist, including porous and upholstered items, and refuse blanket salvage claims.
Identify waste and environmental obligations and refer disposal to licensed handlers.
Identify the jurisdiction whose rules apply and flag where local rules are unresolved or have changed.
Refuse zero-contamination or clearance statements that have not been verified by a competent authority.
Prepare a privacy-conscious, scope-limited handover that avoids disclosure of personal medical or drug-use information.

instruction.heading: Module authority and restricted work
instruction.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a property, investigate it, collect or test any sample, carry out decontamination or remediation, transport or dispose of waste, or issue any clearance, certificate or statement that a property is free of contamination. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate, approval or authority. Investigation, sampling, remediation and clearance are restricted work for suitably qualified and, where required, licensed professionals acting under a written plan. Police, regulatory and other official authority may control a site, and their release must be obtained in writing where it applies. Owner, manager, tenant or insurer permission does not replace it. In every case, stop and refer if the authority, the hazard or the qualification is uncertain.

instruction.heading: 1. Scope, scene history and limits
instruction.body: Scope, scene history and limits is a decision and documentation competence. It is not permission to carry out hazardous remediation. The first task is to distinguish suspected drug use, storage and manufacturing, because each suggests a different risk pathway and a different response. Do not judge the level of residue from its appearance. Establish the task boundary through an employer-approved procedure, verified site information and an appropriately qualified specialist, before accepting any physical work. Record each claim with its date and source. Separate what was directly observed from what was reported, and list each question that is still unanswered. Unknown conditions stay recorded as unknown. They are never treated as proof of safety. In a scenario where a property manager wants same-day service with no site history and no contamination assessment, pause access and request a competent screening, the site authority and a written scope.

instruction.heading: 2. Scene authority, permissions and release
instruction.body: Before any progress, confirm who controls access, what written permission exists, whether the police or another relevant authority has released the site where that applies, and whether an independent competent person has assessed the potential hazards. Confirm lawful access, property permission and the protection of occupants. Where the legal position is unclear, pause access. Authority is not established by a key, a verbal assurance or a general building code. Work that is permitted in one jurisdiction may require a licence or independent verification in another, so the local rules must be identified before the authority is treated as settled. Record the authority chain and the referral decision in the job file.

instruction.heading: 3. Contamination routes and uncertainty
instruction.body: Contamination can reach people and surfaces through contact, through inhalation of dust or airborne material, and through cross-transfer on shoes, tools, clothing, bags and vehicles. Identify each route for the premises in front of you, and record the concern without guessing at concentrations, because a concentration cannot be judged from the look of a room or from a smell. Never substitute appearance, odour, a customer's assurance or an unverified reading for an authorised assessment. Uncertainty is itself a reason to pause and refer. In training, distinguish observation from validated laboratory evidence, and record which of the two you actually have.

instruction.heading: 4. Laboratory versus residue-only properties
instruction.body: Residue associated with drug use and contamination from a clandestine laboratory create different risks, different investigations and different remedial needs. Recognition, not analysis, is the skill taught here. Signs that suggest a possible laboratory or manufacturing activity include unusual chemical containers, improvised equipment, strong unexplained chemical odours, heavy staining, or evidence of ventilation or sealing that does not fit the use of a home. If anything of that kind is seen, do not enter further, do not touch or move any item, leave the area, keep others away and contact emergency services or the police and the authorised specialist. Do not attempt to identify or handle the materials yourself. Record what was seen, where and when, and who was notified.

instruction.heading: 5. Independent sampling and chain of custody
instruction.body: Sampling plans, laboratories, sample locations and documented chain of custody are the work of independent professionals. This lesson describes their purpose so that you can recognise when they are needed and can question an unsupported result. It does not train any unqualified person to collect samples. A single sample cannot represent a whole property, and a result from one room does not clear another. When a result is offered without a documented sampling plan, a named laboratory and a custody record, treat it as unverified and ask for competent interpretation before relying on it. In training, identify the representativeness limits in a fictional case and request specialist validation. Do not collect any sample.

instruction.heading: 6. Worker exposure prevention and PPE decisions
instruction.body: Respirators, protective clothing, ventilation and entry controls depend on a formal assessment and on operators who have been trained to use them. A worker who chooses equipment from whatever is available, such as ordinary gloves or a disposable mask, has not met the requirement. Where an exposure is suspected, stop the activity, restrict access to the affected area and follow the employer's incident and medical referral procedure. Do not improvise protection. Do not self-treat beyond first-response steps the employer has approved. Record the time, the people involved and the exposure concern, and keep the record confidential. A safety-critical omission in this area prevents competency sign-off, whatever the test score.

instruction.heading: 7. Containment and cross-contamination
instruction.body: Containment protects the people who are not doing the work as well as the worker. A crew that plans to carry items through an occupied corridor creates a route that can spread contamination, so the route must be assessed before anything is moved. Define the supervised zones and the handoff points on a diagram, and keep clean and possibly contaminated areas apart. Do not move contents through shared spaces or into vehicles until the containment plan has been approved. Stop if public access, migration outside the zone or uncontrolled movement is observed, and reassess the boundary. In training, create a supervised zone and handoff diagram for a fictional property.

instruction.heading: 8. Material classification and specialist decisions
instruction.body: Materials differ in how contamination behaves within them. Hard surfaces, porous materials, upholstered furniture, carpet, textiles and electronic items each need a specialist decision on whether to keep, clean, remove, isolate or investigate further. A customer's demand for universal salvage of upholstered furniture cannot be accepted, because it cannot be supported by the work done. Identify each point at which a specialist decision is needed, and document any exception to the normal decision path together with the person who approved it. In training, identify specialist decision points for a fictional set of items.

instruction.heading: 9. Waste and environmental obligations
instruction.body: Debris from a former laboratory, contaminated materials and other drug-related waste are not ordinary household rubbish. A crew that plans to put unknown former-laboratory debris into residential bins has made an error that must be stopped. Waste must be identified, packaged, transported and disposed of through licensed handlers and approved destinations, under the applicable environmental and waste rules. Document the stop-work decision and the referral to a licensed waste handler, and do not remove any waste until the handler has been engaged and has confirmed the arrangements in writing.

instruction.heading: 10. Country-specific rules and thresholds
instruction.body: Rules about drug contamination, testing and remediation differ between countries and sometimes within them. Those rules must not be applied to Australia, to other countries or to property types they do not cover, and older standards must not be substituted for current rules. Some rules set a numerical threshold for a particular type of premises. The current value and its scope must be obtained from the authority that publishes it, and no value is given in this lesson. Flag any premises rule that is unresolved, and refer it.

instruction.heading: 11. Independent verification and clearance claims
instruction.body: A worker who is asked to sign a certificate of zero contamination must refuse, because no one can truthfully make that statement on the basis of a visit, a wipe, a photograph or a verbal account. Clearance is a decision for a competent, independent party acting under the applicable scheme, using documented sampling and laboratory evidence where the scheme requires it. Specify the competent verification that is needed, record the refusal of the unverified statement and state the limits of what you can confirm. An attractive assurance from a customer does not change this.

instruction.heading: 12. Handover, health concerns and privacy
instruction.body: A handover must be factual, limited to the scope actually done and privacy-conscious. It records the verified facts, the unresolved issues, the referrals made and the scope limits. It does not disclose personal information about a past tenant or occupant, including medical history or drug use, to a customer who asks for it. Those details are sensitive, and disclosure is governed by privacy law and by the authority that holds the record. Refer any such request to the designated manager. If an event has raised a health or exposure concern, stop work, restrict access and follow the local emergency, employer incident and medical referral procedures. Do not promise that a property is free of contamination. In training, prepare a privacy-conscious, scope-limited handover for a fictional job.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
instruction.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: the authority or written release is missing or unclear; the hazard is unknown; a suspected laboratory or manufacturing activity is evident; anyone may have been exposed; a sample, test or result has no documented plan or custody; the PPE has not been approved; a waste route is unlicensed; a party asks for a clearance, a zero-contamination statement or disclosure of personal information; or the applicable jurisdiction is unknown. Stopping is a correct professional decision. Record it, and restart only when the authority has confirmed the scope in writing.

procedure: Stop. Do not enter further, and do not touch, move, open or test anything.
If a suspected laboratory, manufacturing equipment or unusual chemical containers are seen, leave the area, keep others away and contact emergency services or the police.
Confirm in writing the authority that controls access, any release it has given and the boundaries of that release.
If anyone may have been exposed, end the activity and follow the employer's incident and medical referral procedure. Do not self-treat beyond approved first-response steps.
Refer investigation, sampling, remediation, waste and clearance questions to the appropriately qualified and, where required, licensed professional.
Identify the applicable jurisdiction and its current rules.
Record the observations, the sources, the unknowns, the stop-work decision and the referral in the job file.
Issue a scope-limited, privacy-conscious handover. Make no clearance or zero-contamination statement.

workedExamples.situation: A property manager wants same-day service on a rental property with no site history and no contamination assessment.
workedExamples.reasoning: Pause access. Request a competent screening, the site authority and a written scope. Record the request, the unknowns and the referral. Same-day service cannot be justified without these.

workedExamples.situation: A worker enters a property and sees unusual chemical containers, improvised equipment and heavy unexplained staining.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the worker do now?
workedExamples.reasoning: Leave the area without touching anything. Keep others away. Contact emergency services or the police and the authorised specialist. Record what was seen, where, when and who was told. Do not identify or handle the materials.

workedExamples.situation: A crew plans to carry items through an occupied corridor and into a vehicle.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must happen before any item moves?
workedExamples.reasoning: Assess the route, define supervised zones and handoff points on a diagram, and obtain approval for the containment plan. Stop if movement would reach shared or public areas without control.

workedExamples.situation: A customer demands universal salvage of contaminated upholstered furniture.
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse the blanket decision. Each item needs a specialist decision, and any exception needs a documented approval. The customer's demand does not change the required decision path.

workedExamples.situation: A worker is asked to sign a certificate that a property has zero contamination.
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse. The statement cannot be made on the basis of a visit, a wipe or a verbal account. Specify the competent, independent verification required and record the refusal.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks for the medical history and drug-use details of a previous tenant.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not disclose. The information is sensitive and its release is governed by privacy law and the authority that holds the record. Refer the request to the designated manager and record it.

equipmentAndPpe: PPE selected from a formal assessment by a qualified person, with fit, compatibility and removal training verified by the employer.
Respiratory protection only where the formal assessment requires it, used by trained operators with fit verified under the employer's program.
Supervised zone markers, barrier tape and a documented handoff diagram.
Sealed, labelled containers for any waste that a licensed handler has approved, used only under the handler's instructions.
Records: job file, observation log, referral record, stop-work record, exposure report and privacy-conscious handover.
Training-only props and paper records. No real drug residue, no real laboratory equipment, no sampling and no chemicals are used in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Starting work on a rental or residential property because the manager or owner has asked for it.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the authority, the written release and the scope before any step. Pause if they are missing.

commonErrors.error: Judging the level of contamination from the appearance, a smell or a customer's word.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the observation as unverified and refer for competent assessment.

commonErrors.error: Touching or moving items at a suspected laboratory, or staying to look around.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave, keep others away and contact emergency services or the police and the authorised specialist.

commonErrors.error: Taking a single sample or result as proof for the whole property.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat it as unverified until the sampling plan, the laboratory and the chain of custody are documented and interpreted by a competent person.

commonErrors.error: Putting former-laboratory debris into residential bins.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop. Engage a licensed waste handler and obtain written arrangements before any removal.

commonErrors.error: Applying an older standard, or another country's rule, to the property.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify the current rule for the applicable jurisdiction, and flag any rule that is unresolved.

commonErrors.error: Signing a zero-contamination or clearance certificate.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse the statement. Specify the independent competent verification required.

commonErrors.error: Telling a customer about a previous tenant's medical or drug-use history.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not disclose. Refer the request to the designated manager.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This module does not grant authority to enter, investigate, sample, decontaminate, transport or dispose of material, or to issue any clearance. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.
Investigation, sampling, remediation, waste handling and clearance are restricted work for suitably qualified and, where required, licensed professionals.
Police, regulatory and other official release must be obtained in writing where it applies. Owner, manager, tenant and insurer permission do not replace it.
US guidance is voluntary and is not federal cleanup law, and no Australian equivalent is confirmed for it. New Zealand rules are not Australian law.

A numerical contamination threshold exists in some rules for some premises. No value is given in this lesson. Use the current value from the publishing authority, and never transfer a value from one jurisdiction or property type to another.
No process, product, quantity, dilution, sampling method or decontamination method is given. Recipes and processing for drugs or chemicals are not provided and are outside this module.
Privacy law governs disclosure of personal information about occupants and former occupants. This lesson does not authorise any disclosure.

qualityStandard: The learner identifies the authority, the written release and the unknowns in a given case and states the decision that follows.
The learner distinguishes observation from validated evidence and refuses to rely on appearance, odour or assurance.
The learner recognises the signs that call for leaving the area and escalating, without touching or identifying materials.
The learner identifies the applicable jurisdiction and flags unresolved or changed rules.
The learner refuses zero-contamination and clearance statements and specifies the competent verification required.
The learner prepares a privacy-conscious, scope-limited handover for a fictional case with no personal information disclosed.
documentationEvidence: Scope and authority record: controlling party, written release, boundaries, unknowns and the named reviewer.
Observation log with the date, source and whether each item is observed or reported.
Stop-work and referral record, including the emergency or police notification where it applies.
Exposure report and medical referral record, held confidentially.
PPE assessment and approval record, and the competency record for each worker.
Containment plan with the supervised zones and handoff diagram.
Waste referral record with the licensed handler's written arrangements.
Jurisdiction and rule-check record, with unresolved items flagged.
Privacy-conscious, scope-limited handover with verified facts, unresolved issues, referrals and limits.
summary: Drug-contamination work is a referral-first area. Authority and written release come first.
Appearance, odour and assurance are not evidence. Record unknowns as unknowns.
A suspected laboratory means leave, do not touch, and escalate to emergency services or the police and specialists.
Sampling, testing and clearance belong to independent, qualified professionals with documented custody.
PPE is formally assessed and trained for. Improvised protection is refused.
Containment and handoff are planned before anything moves.
Waste goes only to licensed handlers under written arrangements.
Identify the current rule for the applicable jurisdiction. Do not transfer rules or values between places.
Refuse zero-contamination claims. Protect privacy in every handover.

knowledgeChecks.question: A property manager wants same-day drug-contamination service with no site history and no assessment. What is the correct response?
options: Start the job, because the manager has the keys and the work needs to begin the same day
Pause access and request competent screening, site authority and a written scope.
Complete a quick visual check and then decide whether the job can go ahead on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker finds unusual chemical containers, improvised equipment and strong chemical odours in a house. What should the worker do?
options: Photograph the equipment and keep working in the other rooms, since the hazard is only in one room
Move the containers outside to ventilate the house, so the smell clears before the next visit
Leave the area without touching anything, keep others away and contact emergency services or the police.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker is shown a good-looking room and told it is clean. What is the correct view?
options: Appearance and assurance are not evidence. The room stays unverified until assessed.
The room is clean, because the customer has said so and the customer knows the room best
The room is clean if it does not smell, since a clean smell is a good sign of a clean room

knowledgeChecks.question: A crew is asked to plan the movement of items through an occupied corridor. What must happen first?
options: Move the items quickly before anyone is in the corridor, so the route is clear for the crew
Assess the route, define the supervised zones and handoff points, and get the containment plan approved.
Ask the occupants to stay in their rooms and proceed with the move, since they will not be in the way

knowledgeChecks.question: A single sample from one room is offered as proof that a whole property is clear. What is correct?
options: Accept it, because a sample is a scientific test and the result is trusted by the authorities and the courts for every room in the property
Accept it for the room sampled and assume the rest of the property is clear, since the sample was taken carefully
Treat it as unverified until the sampling plan, laboratory and custody record are documented and interpreted by a competent person.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker has no approved PPE but has ordinary gloves and a disposable mask. What is the response?
options: Stop, because PPE must come from a formal assessment and trained use, and improvised protection is refused.
Proceed carefully with the gloves and mask, since the worker is trained to use them with care
Proceed if the supervisor is nearby and can see the worker from the door of the room at all times

knowledgeChecks.question: A crew wants to put former-laboratory debris into residential bins. What is correct?
options: Do it, because household bins are collected every week and the debris will be gone soon
Stop. Engage a licensed waste handler and get written arrangements before any removal.
Do it if the debris is bagged and sealed properly before it goes into the bin

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer demands that all the upholstered furniture in a contaminated house be salvaged. What is the response?
options: Agree, because the customer has asked and the customer is paying for the whole job in full today
Agree for all furniture that looks clean and has no stains, odour or marks on it at all in the house
Refuse the blanket decision. Each item needs a specialist decision, and exceptions need documented approval.

knowledgeChecks.question: A rental property is assessed using an older standard without checking the current New Zealand rental rules. What is the correct response?
options: Identify the current rule for the applicable jurisdiction and flag anything unresolved. Do not substitute an older standard.
The older standard applies, because it is the one the assessor knows well and has used for years on other jobs
Apply the New Zealand rule to any Australian property, because it is the newest rule available to the assessor today

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker is asked to sign a certificate of zero contamination after a visit and a wipe. What is correct?
options: Sign it, because the worker has done the visit and has a record of the wipe on the day
Refuse. Specify the competent, independent verification required and record the refusal.
Sign it with a note that the property is clear for today, since the wipe was clean

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer asks for the medical history and drug-use details of a former tenant. What is the response?
options: Provide them, because the customer owns the property and can ask for any record
Provide only the drug-use details, since they are less sensitive
Do not disclose. Refer the request to the designated manager and record it.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker may have been exposed during a task. What must happen?
options: End the activity, follow the employer's incident and medical referral procedure, and keep the record confidential.
Continue the task and report at the end of the day, since the exposure is probably minor and nothing has happened yet
Self-treat with a household product and continue if no symptoms appear, since most exposures settle quickly on their own

officialReferences.covers: WA Department of Health page, read through a summary tool. Describes a best-practice guide for testing, remediating and validating a contaminated property, and recommends that testing and remediation are done by different companies. The page does not mention a licence, a licensing scheme or an environmental health officer; it says testing and remediation companies need the necessary competencies. Publisher: WA Department of Health.

officialReferences.title: Clandestine drug laboratories and cleaning contamination
officialReferences.pageDate: Last reviewed 22-05-2026 (no published or updated date shown)
officialReferences.covers: WA Department of Health page, read through a summary tool, at the health.wa.gov.au address (the healthywa address in the source list was not fetched). Says that meth manufacturing sites are the highest-risk type; residues are tested, remediated if above health investigation levels, then re-tested; occupants should not enter or clean the property themselves and should use qualified environmental professionals; records are kept; home insurance is checked first; suspected drug manufacturing is reported to WA Police. Publisher: WA Department of Health.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines on meth contamination

Covers landlord and tenant duties, contamination thresholds, approved testing, and decontamination under regulations based on NZS 8510:2017. Numerical thresholds are not reproduced in this lesson. Publisher: New Zealand Tenancy Services (MBIE).
